semantics.note: Firm 'will take years' forecast. 'Even if OpenAI pays' is a robustness qualifier, not an antecedent; it is preserved. No deadline was stated.

contract.note: The plain reading of periodic project profit is ordinary. Requiring proof of timely payment before support is stricter than 'even if' implies, since late payment would only strengthen the claim. It does not change the current result.

evidence.note: Oracle disclosure on prepaid and customer-supplied hardware in aggregate. It does not identify OpenAI payments or Stargate project profit.

reviews.rationale: Firm forecast with no stated deadline. The packet has no Stargate-level profit data and no conclusive event, only consolidated Oracle results, which the contract excludes. Not enough has happened to score the forecast.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion, responding to Oracle's tweet.

semantics.note: Captures both parts: power for only two buildings, and not on schedule as of late April 2026.

contract.note: Comparing against the applicable schedule and not counting future deadlines as missed is a fair, ordinary reading.

evidence.note: Oracle's own statement. It confirms 200MW operational, consistent with two buildings, and asserts on schedule. Company self-disclosure gives no milestone baseline.
Independent Epoch estimate that buildings 3-4 were later than expected and the campus is 3-6 months behind the mid-2026 target. It is an uncertain projection, not a record of a missed milestone.
Crusoe 2025 timetable: two-building phase of about 200MW, and full campus targeted for mid-2026, which was still ahead in April.

reviews.rationale: The two-building/200MW part is consistent with e1 and e3. The central 'not on schedule' claim is not established. No dated milestone record shows a missed April obligation. Epoch's delay is an uncertain projection, and the mid-2026 completion date had not yet passed. Oracle's denial is self-disclosure.

semantics.note: Faithful to the model and its premises, though it says 'margin' where the source says 'gross margin'. The contract restores the gross-margin label.

contract.note: The speaker named the metric 'gross margin', so testing both the arithmetic and that label is fair to his words.

evidence.note: Amortisation recomputed from his premises gives $54.13M/month, $649.6M/yr, ~5.15% and ~-40.3%. The arithmetic holds.
The standard definition of gross profit excludes financing. Gross margin on his inputs is at most about 21%, not -40%. Deducting principal alongside depreciation also double-counts.

reviews.rationale: The loan payments and percentages reproduce from his stated premises. Calling them 'gross margin' is wrong: interest and principal repayment do not belong in gross profit, which would be about 21% on his own costs. The arithmetic part holds; the gross-margin characterisation does not.

attribution.note: Zitron's own accusation in his post.

semantics.note: Wording is faithful. The core claim is about the real reason for a decision and about deceptive intent, which is causal rather than a plain observation. 'Nothingburger' is evaluative.

contract.note: Reading 'lied' as knowing misrepresentation with capacity as the true reason is the ordinary meaning. Leaving 'nothingburger' unscored is appropriate.

evidence.note: Anthropic's stated safeguards rationale. Company disclosure; it does not show sincerity either way.
Shows general capacity expansion and strain. It does not link capacity to the Mythos decision.
Independent AISI tests show a real cyber-capability advance, so the safety concern had an empirical basis. Says nothing on motive.

reviews.rationale: No decision records or firsthand accounts show capacity caused the restriction or that Anthropic knowingly misstated its reason. The independent AISI results show a real capability basis but do not rebut capacity as a factor. The evidence settles neither side.
